nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-01.title: Thales circle
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-01.body:
$\angle APB = 90^\circ$ exactly when $P$ lies on the circle with diameter $AB$. Its center is the midpoint $\left(\frac{21}{2}, 10\right)$ and its diameter is $AB=\sqrt{21^2+20^2}=29$, so the radius is $\frac{29}{2}$. The leftmost point of the circle has $a = \frac{21}{2}-\frac{29}{2} = -4$ (the point $(-4,10)$).

**Answer: $-4$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-02.title: Odd number of divisors
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-02.body:
Splitting the balls equally between two people left exactly one ball, so the number of divisors is odd. Only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors, and the only square between 1900 and 2000 is $44^2 = 1936 = 2^4\cdot 11^2$. Its odd divisors are the divisors of $11^2$: $1, 11, 121$. Any of them could be Cindy's ball.

**Answer: $1, 11, 121$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-03.title: Eliminate x and y
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-03.body:
From the second equation $y = 2-\frac1z = \frac{2z-1}{z}$. Then $x = 1-\frac1y = 1-\frac{z}{2z-1} = \frac{z-1}{2z-1}$. The third equation becomes
$$z + \frac{2z-1}{z-1} = -3 \;\Longrightarrow\; z(z-1)+2z-1 = -3(z-1) \;\Longrightarrow\; z^2+4z-4=0.$$
So $z = \frac{-4\pm\sqrt{32}}{2} = -2\pm\sqrt8$. Both values work (neither makes a denominator zero).

**Answer: $(A,B)=(-2,8)$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-04.title: Count working cases
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-04.body:
The first machine works when at most one part fails. With the $\frac35$-part failing, the other two must both work; otherwise at most one of the $p$-parts may fail:
$$P_1 = \tfrac35(1-p)^2 + \tfrac25\left[(1-p)^2 + 2p(1-p)\right] = (1-p)^2+\tfrac45p(1-p) = \tfrac15p^2-\tfrac65p+1.$$
The second machine works with probability $1-(p^2-p+1) = p-p^2$. Setting them equal:
$$\tfrac15p^2-\tfrac65p+1 = p-p^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; 6p^2-11p+5=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; (6p-5)(p-1)=0.$$
So $p=\frac56$, or $p=1$ (in which case both machines always fail).

**Answer: $p=\frac56$ (also $p=1$)**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-05.title: Vieta's formulas
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-05.body:
Let the roots be $a,b$. Then $a+b=-\frac4A$ and $ab=\frac3A$. So
$$a^2+b^2=(a+b)^2-2ab=\frac{16}{A^2}-\frac6A,\qquad a^3+b^3=(a+b)^3-3ab(a+b)=-\frac{64}{A^3}+\frac{36}{A^2}.$$
Setting them equal and multiplying by $A^3$: $-64+36A = 16A-6A^2$, i.e. $3A^2+10A-32=0$, so $(A-2)(3A+16)=0$.

**Answer: $A=2$ or $A=-\frac{16}{3}$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-06.title: Two equations
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-06.body:
Let the tunnel have length $B$, the train be at distance $T$ from the near end, and let the hero have flown a fraction $F$ of the tunnel, so he is $(1-F)B$ from the near end (the end the train is approaching) and $FB$ from the far end.

- Flying to the near end: $\frac{(1-F)B}{30} = \frac{T}{200}$.
- Flying back to the far end: $\frac{FB}{30} = \frac{B+T}{200}$.

Subtracting the first from the second: $\frac{(2F-1)B}{30} = \frac{B}{200}$, so $2F-1 = \frac{3}{20}$ and $F = \frac{23}{40}$.

**Answer: $\frac{23}{40}$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-06.title: Relative timing
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-06.body:
Whatever the hero does, the train covers the tunnel length in the extra time it takes him to fly the extra distance. Going to the far end instead of the near end, the hero flies an extra $FB-(1-F)B=(2F-1)B$ at 30 mph, while the train goes an extra $B$ at 200 mph. So $(2F-1)\cdot\frac{200}{30}=1$, $2F-1=\frac{3}{20}$, $F=\frac{23}{40}$.

**Answer: $\frac{23}{40}$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-07.title: Multiply the sums
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-07.body:
$$(\cos A+\cos B)(\sin A+\sin B) = \sin A\cos A + \sin B\cos B + (\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B) = \tfrac12(\sin2A+\sin2B)+\sin(A+B).$$
So $\frac18 = -\frac{27}{40} + \sin(A+B)$, giving $\sin(A+B) = \frac{5}{40}+\frac{27}{40} = \frac45$.

**Answer: $\frac45$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-07.title: Sum-to-product
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-07.body:
$\cos A+\cos B = 2\cos\frac{A+B}2\cos\frac{A-B}2$ and $\sin A+\sin B = 2\sin\frac{A+B}2\cos\frac{A-B}2$, so $\tan\frac{A+B}{2} = \frac{1/4}{1/2} = \frac12$. Then $\sin(A+B) = \frac{2\tan\frac{A+B}2}{1+\tan^2\frac{A+B}2} = \frac{1}{5/4} = \frac45$.

**Answer: $\frac45$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-09.title: Set area equal to perimeter
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-09.body:
With side $s$, the figure consists of the triangle and three semicircles of radius $\frac s2$:
$$\text{Area} = \frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2 + 3\cdot\frac{\pi}{8}s^2 = \frac{(2\sqrt3+3\pi)s^2}{8}.$$
The boundary is three semicircular arcs: $\text{Perimeter}=3\cdot\frac{\pi s}{2}$. Equating, $s=\frac{12\pi}{3\pi+2\sqrt3}$. Rationalizing with $3\pi-2\sqrt3$:
$$s=\frac{12\pi(3\pi-2\sqrt3)}{9\pi^2-12}=\frac{4\pi(3\pi-2\sqrt3)}{3\pi^2-4}=\frac{12\pi\cdot\pi-8\pi\sqrt3}{3\pi^2-4}.$$

**Answer: $(a,b)=(12\pi,-8\pi)$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-10.title: Choose letters around the third
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-10.body:
If the third letter is the $k$-th letter of the alphabet, choose 2 of the $k-1$ earlier letters for the first two places and 1 of the $26-k$ later letters for the last place: $\binom{k-1}{2}(26-k)$ ways.

- N ($k=14$): $\binom{13}2\cdot12=936$
- Y ($k=25$): $\binom{24}2\cdot1=276$
- C ($k=3$): $\binom22\cdot23=23$
- M ($k=13$): $\binom{12}2\cdot13=858$
- L ($k=12$): $\binom{11}2\cdot14=770$

Total: $936+276+23+858+770=2863$.

**Answer: 2863**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-12.title: Angle sums in two triangles
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-12.body:
Let $\angle CAM=\angle BAN=\alpha$ and $\angle CBN=\angle ABM=\beta$. In triangle $AMB$, $\angle MAB = A-\alpha$ and $\angle MBA=\beta$, so $\angle AMB = 180^\circ-(A-\alpha)-\beta$. In triangle $ANB$, $\angle NAB=\alpha$ and $\angle NBA = B-\beta$, so $\angle ANB=180^\circ-\alpha-(B-\beta)$. Adding,
$$200^\circ = 360^\circ - A - B = 180^\circ + (180^\circ-A-B) = 180^\circ+\angle ACB.$$
So $\angle ACB = 20^\circ$.

**Answer: $20^\circ$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-13.title: Split into two geometric series
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-13.body:
The $k$-th term ($k=0,1,2,\dots$) is $\frac{3^k+1}{9^k} = \left(\frac13\right)^k+\left(\frac19\right)^k$. So the sum is
$$\frac{1}{1-\frac13}+\frac{1}{1-\frac19}=\frac32+\frac98=\frac{21}8.$$

**Answer: $\frac{21}{8}$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-15.title: Rationalize
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-15.body:
$$\frac{\sqrt5-\sqrt3+\sqrt2}{\sqrt5+\sqrt3+\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt5-\sqrt3+\sqrt2}{\sqrt5-\sqrt3+\sqrt2}=\frac{(\sqrt5+\sqrt2-\sqrt3)^2}{(\sqrt5+\sqrt2)^2-3}=\frac{10+2\sqrt{10}-2\sqrt{15}-2\sqrt6}{4+2\sqrt{10}}.$$
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $2\sqrt{10}-4$ simplifies this to $\frac{\sqrt{10}-\sqrt6}{2}$. Hence $2\cdot\frac{\sqrt5-\sqrt3+\sqrt2}{\sqrt5+\sqrt3+\sqrt2}=\sqrt{10}-\sqrt6$.

**Answer: $(10,6)$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-16.title: Powers of 2 in (T-1)(T+1)
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-16.body:
$T$ must be odd. Then $T-1$ and $T+1$ are consecutive even numbers, so exactly one of them is divisible by 4 and the other contributes only one factor of 2. For $2^8\mid(T-1)(T+1)$ we need $2^7\mid T-1$ or $2^7\mid T+1$, i.e. $T\equiv\pm1\pmod{128}$.

- $T=1+128k$ with $0\le k\le15$: 16 values (up to $1921$).
- $T=-1+128k$ with $1\le k\le15$: 15 values (up to $1919$).

Total $16+15=31$.

**Answer: 31**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-17.title: Ptolemy's theorem
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-17.body:
For P on minor arc AB, $APBC$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals $AB$ and $PC$. Ptolemy gives $AB\cdot PC = AP\cdot BC + BP\cdot CA$, i.e. $6z = 11x+7y$. So $m=\frac{11}6$, $n=\frac76$ and $m+n=\frac{18}{6}=3$.

**Answer: 3**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-19.title: Choose the digits
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-19.body:
Any 5 distinct digits from $\{0,1,\dots,9\}$ can be arranged in decreasing order in exactly one way, and the first digit is then the largest, so it is never 0. Hence the count is $\binom{10}{5}=252$.

**Answer: 252**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-20.title: Vieta with roots a/r, a, ar
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-20.body:
Let the roots be $\frac ar, a, ar$. Then
$$a\left(\tfrac1r+1+r\right) = -\tfrac{92}{19},\qquad a^2\left(\tfrac1r+1+r\right)=\tfrac{23}{19}.$$
Dividing, $a = \frac{23}{-92} = -\frac14$. The product of the roots is $a^3 = -\frac1{64} = -\frac{T}{19}$, so $T=\frac{19}{64}$.

**Answer: $\frac{19}{64}$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-22.title: Distance to the line
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-22.body:
$x^2+y^2$ is the squared distance from the origin to $(x,y)$ on the line. The distance from the origin to $20x+21y=1247$ is $\frac{1247}{\sqrt{20^2+21^2}}=\frac{1247}{29}=43$. So the minimum is $43^2=1849$.

**Answer: 1849**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-23.title: Factor out x - 1
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-23.body:
The sum of the coefficients is $f(1)=0$, so $f(x)=(x-1)g(x)$ with $g$ having integer coefficients. Then $f(1992)=1991\,g(1992)$ is always a multiple of $1991=11\cdot181$. Taking $f(x)=x-1$ shows $T$ must divide $1991$. The smallest such $T>1$ is $11$.

**Answer: 11**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-24.title: Triangle of medians
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-24.body:
The medians of a triangle form a triangle whose area is $\frac34$ of the original: $\frac34\cdot3\sqrt{15}=\frac{9\sqrt{15}}4$. If $\theta$ is the angle between the sides 3 and 6 of the median triangle, $\frac12\cdot3\cdot6\sin\theta=\frac{9\sqrt{15}}{4}$, so $\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{15}}4$ and $\cos\theta=\pm\frac14$. By the law of cosines the third median $k$ satisfies
$$k^2 = 9+36\mp2\cdot3\cdot6\cdot\tfrac14 = 36\text{ or }54.$$
If $k=6$, two medians are equal, which makes the triangle isosceles. Since it is scalene, $k=\sqrt{54}=3\sqrt6$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt6$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-26.title: Equal heights
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-26.body:
Triangles $ACB$ and $ACD$ share base $AC$, which lies on $y=x$, so they have equal area exactly when $B$ and $D$ are the same distance from that line. $B$ satisfies $y-x=31$. For $ABCD$ to be a quadrilateral, $D$ is on the other side of $AC$, on the reflected line $x-y=31$. Hence $a-b=31$.

**Answer: 31**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-28.title: Sum the series and factor
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-28.body:
For convergence $a,b\ge2$, and $A=\frac{a}{a-1}$, $B=\frac b{b-1}$. Then $\frac a{a-1}+\frac b{b-1}=\frac{15}7$ becomes $7(2ab-a-b)=15(ab-a-b+1)$, i.e. $ab-8a-8b+15=0$, so
$$(a-8)(b-8)=49.$$
With $a>b\ge2$ the factorizations give $(a-8,b-8)=(49,1)$, i.e. $(57,9)$; the other options $(-1,-49)$ and $(-7,-7)$ give $b\le1$ or $a=b$. Check: $\frac{57}{56}+\frac98=\frac{120}{56}=\frac{15}7$.

**Answer: $(57,9)$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-29.title: Substitute s = sin + cos
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-29.body:
Let $s=\sin\theta+\cos\theta$. Then $s^2=1+\sin2\theta$, so the equation is $s=s^2$: $s=0$ or $s=1$.

- $s=0$: $\tan\theta=-1$, $\theta=135^\circ,315^\circ$.
- $s=1$: $\sqrt2\sin(\theta+45^\circ)=1$, so $\theta+45^\circ=45^\circ,135^\circ,405^\circ$, giving $\theta=0^\circ,90^\circ,360^\circ$.

**Answer: $0^\circ,90^\circ,135^\circ,315^\circ,360^\circ$**

nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-30.title: Remove the absolute value
nyciml-1992-93-fall-seniora-30.body:
If $m>n$, $F=\frac72(m+n)+\frac32(m-n)=5m+2n$. Solving $5m+2n=1992$: $n\equiv1\pmod5$, so $(m,n)=(398-2t,\,5t+1)$. We need $m>n$: $398-2t>5t+1$, so $t\le56$; and $t\ge0$ for $n\ge1$. That is 57 pairs. If $m=n$, $7m=1992$ has no integer solution. If $m<n$, by symmetry there are another 57 pairs. Total $114$.

**Answer: 114**
